checks.label: We can add phasor voltages and phasor currents graphically, exactly the same as if we were adding vectors: every sum of currents or voltages drawn is the nose-to-tail sum of its arrows, found by the same rule as the sum of the pulls

Sinusoids of different frequencies cannot be represented on the same phasor diagram, because at any instant in time the phase angle between them is different: on the two-speed screen the angle between the arrows changes from each moment to the next
You can divide phasors: wherever the current's tip is dragged on the dividing screen, the impedance drawn is the voltage divided by the current, with the sizes divided and the angles taken away

The turning arrow's shadow on the upright line is its height, and the wave beside it has that same height at the same moment, all the way round; with two currents turning together, the sum's height is always the two heights added
Three equal currents 120° apart close their chain and leave nothing on the neutral at every size; with two at 10 A, shrinking the third opens a gap as big as the amount it shrank

Every number follows from the rule: 20 × 90 ÷ 360 = 5 ms; √(3² + 3²) = 4.24 kN and 4.24 A; √(6² + 8²) = 10 A; in 5 ms the arrows turn 90° and 270°, 180° apart; 230 ÷ 10 = 23 at 0° − (−30°) = 30°; 230 ÷ 5 = 46 at 60°; three 10 A currents leave 0 A; 10, 10 and 4 A leave 6 A; 10, 8 and 6 A leave 3.46 A; 230∠0° − 230∠−120° = 398∠30° V; and every wrong answer offered is a slip worked from the same values
Every puzzle offers three different answers with exactly one accepted, gives each wrong one its own hint, and draws a wrong pick in red but a right one without
Before Check no puzzle's picture shows its answer, and a right answer shows it
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion within 2.5 s
